# name: # Inputs that must raise a parse error. `expected` uses the literal token
# "ERROR" (optionally ":code" for a specific error code) to indicate that
# XML 1.0 well-formedness constraints the lexer enforces directly. Each
# raises its own code rather than a generic rejection, so each is pinned by
# code -- the code is the contract across runtimes, the message is not.
# `]]>` is forbidden in CharData (XML 1.0 2.4) but NOT in AttValue, so the
# input has to place it in element content. A bare `]]>` outside any
# element fails earlier, and more generally, as text_at_top_level.
# `--` may not appear inside a comment (XML 1.0 2.5).
# An attribute name may not repeat within one element (XML 1.0 3.1).
# `<` may not appear literally in an attribute value (XML 1.0 3.1).
# A processing instruction needs a target Name (XML 1.0 2.6).
# Characters outside the Char production are rejected wherever they can
# appear. One row per call site: the census counts CODES, so it would go
# green on the first of these while the other four paths stayed untested.
# U+0001 is written with the \uXXXX escape both runners decode (see
# bom.tsv) -- a literal control byte in a .tsv does not survive editing.
# An unbound namespace prefix violates Namespaces in XML 1.0, which is a
# SEPARATE spec from XML 1.0 well-formedness: `<foo:b/>` is a well-formed
# XML document. The check is therefore opt-in via `strictNamespaces`; the
# default (accepting) behaviour is pinned in namespaces.tsv.
# A namespace name is a URI reference (Namespaces in XML 1.0 §2), and a URI
# reference cannot contain white space. Attribute-value normalisation
# (§3.3.3) turns a literal line break in the declaration into a space
# first, so both spellings land on the same error.
# Error templates must interpolate. The `msg` column pins the rendered
# text, so a template that reverts to a literal `$fsrc` / `$openname`
# placeholder fails here instead of shipping.

msg: closing tag does not match opening tag
closing tag </c> does not match opening tag <b>
